mcqs.q: A Class V preparation is located on the:
opts: Gingival (cervical) third of the facial or lingual surface
mcqs.explain: Class V preparations are on the gingival third of the facial or lingual surface of any tooth.

mcqs.q: Class V preparations can occur on:
mcqs.explain: Class V lesions occur on the cervical third of the facial/lingual surface of all teeth.

mcqs.q: A Class V preparation becomes a COMPOUND preparation when it:
opts: Involves a mesial or distal surface
mcqs.explain: A simple Class V becomes compound when it extends to involve the mesial or distal surface.

mcqs.q: How many walls does a Class V preparation have?
mcqs.explain: A Class V has 5 walls (occlusal/incisal, gingival, mesial, distal, axial), 8 line angles and 4 point angles.

mcqs.q: In a posterior Class V, the 'incisal' wall is renamed the:
mcqs.explain: For posterior teeth, the incisal wall of the Class V is termed the occlusal wall.

mcqs.q: Which material is MOST often used for cervical lesions of anterior/premolar teeth?
mcqs.explain: Because of esthetic demands, composites are most frequently used for cervical lesions of anterior and premolar teeth.

mcqs.q: Microfilled composite is chosen for some Class V defects because it provides:
opts: Increased smoothness and flexibility under cervical flexure
mcqs.explain: Microfilled composite gives smoother surface and flexibility when the tooth flexes cervically (helpful in abfraction lesions).

mcqs.q: Which material is preferred for a high-caries-risk patient with a root-surface Class V lesion?
mcqs.explain: RMGI and compomer (fluoride-releasing) can be used in high-caries-risk patients and for lesions extending onto the root surface.

mcqs.q: An ABFRACTION cervical lesion is caused by:
mcqs.explain: Abfraction is a non-carious cervical lesion attributed to tooth flexure from occlusal stress; abrasion is mechanical wear and erosion is acid-related.

mcqs.q: A cervical lesion caused by ACID (dietary/gastric) is termed:
mcqs.explain: Erosion is chemical (acid) loss of tooth structure; abrasion is mechanical and abfraction is flexural.

mcqs.q: ABRASION of the cervical area is due to:
mcqs.explain: Abrasion is mechanical wear, classically from aggressive horizontal toothbrushing with abrasive paste.

mcqs.q: Class V preparation (like Class III/IV) involves creating access, removing the defect, and:
opts: Making a convenience form for the restoration
mcqs.explain: Class V preparation creates access to the defect, removes the defect, and makes a convenience form for restoration.

mcqs.q: For a small/moderate Class V NOT on the root surface, the objective is to:
mcqs.explain: Small/moderate non-root lesions should be restored as conservatively as possible, extending into dentin only when the defect warrants.

mcqs.q: The three Class V cavity designs are:
mcqs.explain: Class V designs are conventional, beveled conventional, and modified.

mcqs.q: The CONVENTIONAL Class V design (box form) is mainly used for:
mcqs.explain: The conventional (box) design is used for root-surface or larger lesions, often where there is no enamel margin.

mcqs.q: The MODIFIED Class V design is:
opts: A scooped/saucer-shaped conservative prep for small lesions
mcqs.explain: The modified design is a conservative, scooped/saucer-shaped preparation for small lesions, relying on bonding.

mcqs.q: Primary retention of a Class V composite is provided by:
mcqs.explain: Class V composites are retained mainly by the adhesive bond; mechanical grooves are added only for larger/root cases.

mcqs.q: Retention grooves in a Class V are placed in the:
opts: Occlusal/incisal and gingival walls (for larger/root lesions)
mcqs.explain: When extra retention is needed, small grooves are cut along the occlusal/incisal and gingival walls (e.g. root-surface lesions).

mcqs.q: Isolation/retraction for a Class V restoration may use a:
mcqs.explain: A cervical matrix and/or gingival retraction helps isolate the cervical field and adapt/contour the composite.

mcqs.q: The finished restoration shown is a:
mcqs.explain: The image shows a finished cervical (Class V) composite restoration.

mcqs.q: Beveling the enamel margin of a Class V (beveled conventional) aims to:
opts: Increase bonding surface area at the enamel margin
mcqs.explain: The beveled conventional design bevels the enamel margins to increase the etched surface area for bonding.

mcqs.q: Besides esthetics, which factor guides Class V material choice?
opts: Caries risk, access, salivary function and moisture control
mcqs.explain: Material selection also considers caries activity/risk, access to the lesion, salivary function and moisture control.

saqs.q: Define a Class V lesion and when it becomes compound.
saqs.a: On the gingival third of the facial/lingual surface of any tooth; compound when it involves a mesial/distal surface.

saqs.q: Name the three non-carious cervical lesions and their cause.
Why is microfilled composite chosen for some Class V lesions?
saqs.a: It gives increased smoothness and flexibility under cervical flexure (e.g. abfraction).

saqs.q: Which materials suit a high-caries-risk / root-surface Class V?
List the steps of Class V preparation design.
saqs.a: Create access → remove the defect → make a convenience form; conservative, into dentin only if warranted.

saqs.q: Name the three Class V designs and one indication each.
How is a Class V composite retained?
saqs.a: Mainly by the adhesive bond; small retention grooves (occlusal/gingival walls) for larger/root lesions.
